Some things here are not seriously disputed. People do experience persistent symptoms after these infections; that's documented across continents, across multiple outbreaks, and in large longitudinal cohorts, including a cohort of nearly ten thousand participants enrolled in the NIH's RECOVER initiative. It is a substantial share of those infected, though not everyone: U.S. self-report survey data puts current long COVID at roughly six to seven percent of all adults, while a global modeling effort estimated well over a hundred million people experienced at least one persistent symptom cluster in 2020 and 2021 alone. And these conditions are not simply deconditioning or psychological illness. The delayed, prolonged post-exertional crash does not fit the pattern of ordinary fatigue or a typical exercise response, and people with these conditions often had no psychiatric illness before infection; where psychiatric symptoms appear, they are more often a consequence of living with a chronic disabling illness than its cause.
